newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Bond market to tackle new ground under EMU.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Bond market to tackle new ground under EMU.

text.p: Betting on Hungary joining European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) will be the unlikely bond trade of the next century, according to analysts gearing up for a single currency starting in 1999.
While the idea might seem outlandish now, analysts say investors will have to plumb more exotic territority as yield spreads between the lynchpins of the current European bond scene shrink.

Nevertheless, there will still be plenty of ways to make money, they say. Which countries are fudging the EMU criteria and which countries will next make the grade will be the main trade strategies in a "euro bond" market that could eventually rival U.S. Treasuries in size and depth.

"It's going to be a two-way process -- an evaluation of the EMU core and individual countries outside as well," said Andrew McCaffery, joint head of proprietry trading at Yamaichi International in London. "If it is successful, then you do start talking about Poland and Hungary converging also."
EMU is set to begin in 1999 when the European Central Bank (ECB) is put in force and a single monetary policy is put in effect. By 2002, the euro will be introduced and local currencies phased out.
The union is likely to include a small group of EMU cheerleaders at first -- Germany, France, Austria, Luxembourg, Belgium, The Netherlands and possibly, Ireland.
Each country would issue their debt in euros. The mighty German Bund would be replaced by the German euro bond and French OATs by the French euro bond and so on.
The prospect of a single euro bond has sent shivers down some traders' spines.

Volumes would shrink because countries will require less debt if they are meeting the strict fiscal requirements of EMU, one of which is that deficits must be no more than three percent of GDP. Spread differentials, which fuel current bond trade, would evaporate along with the currency risk, leaving credit as the only trade determinant.

"The result is going to be very small differentials, perhaps 10 or 15 basis points," said Adrian Owens, economist at Bank Julius Baer in London. Spreads would likely be measured against the German euro as it becomes the benchmark euro bond.
But Mark Fox, chief European strategist in fixed income at Lehman Brothers in London, said there would still be enough volatility between core euro bonds to feed a healthy amount of trade.

"Unless countries follow absolutely identical policies, you have to let the stress of different policies out somehow. And if you can't do it through currencies, you have to do it through interest rate differentials," he said.

Yamaichi's McCaffery said whether countries are continuing to meet the EMU criteria -- stability pact or not -- would generate volatility in the euro core. "Will they fudge the criteria afterwards? That will cause tension and ramifications," he said.
Short-term money markets would be no less immune to political, fiscal and supply and demand stresses, analysts said.

"Short-term bills of any particular country will still be bid for at local auctions run by the regional central banks of Europe," said Fox. "There's still a possibility some auctions will fail and rates will be bid up or down at different auctions," he said.

Whether the core euro bond market is volatile or stable, analysts said the euro bond market, backed by a population and GDP as big or bigger than that of the United States, could eventually challenge Treasuries in size and liquidity.

Traders envision an environment similar to the U.S. municipal or Canadian provincial debt markets where many different borrowers issue a whole range of debt. Eventually, the ECB may be responsible for some sovereign issues.
John Langton, chief executive of the International Securities Market Association said however, certain conditions must be met for the euro market to thrive.
The number of countries in the first round must be at least six or seven, the euro must be as serious a currency as the yen and dollar, and a full yield curve must be developed.
"If these prerequisites are met, I believe we'll see a lot of investors come into the euro, and we'll see a proper liquid market," said Langton, based in Zurich.

But analysts said the main focus of trade would switch to bonds issued by those outside the EMU core. Convergence trades -- trades which speculate on yield convergence between high-yielding debt markets like Italy and core European bonds like Bunds -- have been in vogue pre-EMU.
Post-EMU, the convergence of bond yields in peripheral countries like Portugal, Poland and Hungary against euro bonds would be the big play, analysts said.
"Investors will be looking to pick up yield by looking outside the core markets into emerging markets, ie. eastern Europe," said Owens at Julius Baer.
This would protect bonds of those countries left outside EMU -- including UK gilts if the British government does not join -- from being seriously undermined, Owens said.
Debt futures markets will also throw up a host of possibilities for bond trades in 2000, analysts said.

The main futures markets in London, Paris and Frankfurt, all hustling to become the main centre of trade, must decide whether there will be one bond future on the various cash bonds or individual futures on each euro cash bond.
"If there is one futures contract, you're going to have bonds of different goverments with different credit ratings all deliverable into the same futures contract," said Fox.
"That means that there is potential for far more complex basis trading...than there is today," he said.
"There's lots and lots of room to make money," said Fox.
